Oracle Fell Nearly 9% as CoreWeave’s Bond Scare Spread

Quick Read

Oracle dropped 9% and lost $38 billion in market value after CoreWeave's bonds spiked to a 15% yield, signaling lenders no longer treat GPU-backed debt as safe.

Oracle's $664 billion backlog and 82% analyst upside hinge on cheap financing, but free cash flow was negative $5 billion last quarter.

Microsoft's $67 billion in free cash flow and interest coverage above 50 make it a safer AI cloud alternative if credit conditions keep tightening.

Just released. Our analysts combed the entire stock market and named the ten best stocks to buy right now, and Oracle didn't make the cut. Enter your email to see the names that beat ORCL. The report is free. Enter your email and see if any of your stocks made the cut.

Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) closed at $130.55, and the average analyst price target stands at $237.97. That puts the implied upside at 82.3%. A gap that wide likely means the consensus has fallen behind the stock, because many targets likely precede the decline.

24/7 Wall Street

Oracle sells database software and enterprise applications. It also sells a growing amount of cloud capacity that AI labs rent to train and run their models. Wall Street watches that last business closely because Oracle has built up $664 billion in remaining performance obligations, a backlog many times larger than its current annual revenue.

Paying for that capacity strains Oracle's balance sheet. Oracle spent $28.5 billion on capital expenditures last quarter, which left free cash flow at negative $5.4 billion. It also plans to raise roughly $40 billion this fiscal year through debt and equity. So when credit markets turn nervous about AI borrowing, Oracle's stock usually falls with them.

CoreWeave's Bond Scare Spread to Oracle Fast

Oracle fell 8.83%, or $12.65 per share. That erased about $38 billion in market value, leaving the company worth $395.76 billion. The stock slid another 2.45% to $127.35 after hours.

On September 30, 2026, CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) chief executive Michael Intrator went on CNBC and said data center regulations would not hurt AI demand and that margins were higher than a year ago. The same day, he sold 78,552 Class A shares of CoreWeave at $87.69, a sale worth at $6,888,224.88. Two weeks later the stock trades at $61.45, and Jim Cramer says owners are scared.

IMDB
Form 4s Show One Sale Outside a Trading Plan

The Form 4 for the September 30 sale (accession 0001769628-26-000441) leaves the 10b5-1 plan box unchecked for all five reported transactions. So the sale was discretionary. The day before, Intrator sold shares at prices from $85.8577 to $90.2553 under a 10b5-1 plan. Those sales were worth more than $26 million, which brings the two days to more than $33 million. He also made plan sales on September 15 and September 22.

A 10b5-1 plan schedules sales ahead of time, and no one has accused Intrator of misconduct. He still holds 21,867,489 Class B shares directly.

Cramer Calls It a "Fire Drill Moment"

title: AI Credit Default Insurance Costs Surge as Investors Assess Data Centre Debt Risks
detail:
AI Credit Default Insurance Costs Surge as Investors Assess Data Centre Debt Risks
Fiona Craig
Thu, October 15, 2026 at 7:07 AM PDT 7 min read
CRWV
ORCL
9984.T
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The cost of protecting against defaults by major US technology companies has risen sharply, reflecting growing investor concerns about debt levels, financing requirements and the potential returns from large-scale artificial intelligence infrastructure investments.

Credit default swap (CDS) spreads for several companies involved in AI development and data centre expansion have reached record levels, according to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence and LSEG.

Oracle (NYSE:ORCL), SoftBank and CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) were among the companies experiencing significant increases in the cost of default protection, as investors reassessed the financial risks associated with AI-related capital expenditure.

The widening spreads suggest that credit markets are placing greater emphasis on the ability of technology companies to generate sufficient cash flow to support their investment programmes and meet debt obligations.

Concerns have been particularly pronounced among data centre operators whose financing arrangements depend partly on anticipated future demand for AI computing capacity.

Oracle Credit Default Swap Spreads Reach Record 288 Basis Points

Oracle recorded a substantial increase in the cost of insuring its debt against default.

According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, the company's five-year credit default swap spread widened by 26 basis points overnight to a record 288 basis points.

The increase reflected a rise in the premium investors were demanding for protection against a potential credit event involving Oracle.

At 288 basis points, the annual cost of CDS protection is approximately $2.88 for every $100 of debt insured, excluding any upfront payments or other contractual adjustments.

The widening spread indicated increased concern about Oracle's credit risk as the company continues to invest in cloud computing and AI infrastructure.

Oracle is among the technology companies committing substantial resources to expanding data centre capacity and computing services to support demand for artificial intelligence applications.

Such investments can require significant upfront expenditure, while the associated revenue and profitability may develop over longer periods.

The increase in default protection costs suggests that investors are paying closer attention to the timing of potential returns and the financial commitments required to support infrastructure expansion.

SoftBank CDS Spreads Widen to 424 Basis Points

SoftBank also experienced a sharp increase in the cost of credit protection.

Investors are losing confidence that revenues from the AI boom will be sufficient to support the vast debt piles financing data centres, pushing bonds backing some of the largest US infrastructure projects into increasingly stressed territory.

Prices of bonds issued to fund prominent data centres where Meta, Nvidia, Oracle and others will become tenants — such as "Hyperion", "Sopaipilla" and "Project Excalibur" — have fallen well below par in recent weeks.

Investors are also dumping debt issued by so-called neocloud companies — of which the best known is Nvidia-backed CoreWeave — who have been the most aggressive in how they finance the AI build-out.

OpenAI's decision to delay its initial public offering until next year and a slowdown in Anthropic's quarterly sales growth have triggered doubts about the sustainability of the AI boom, as analysts point to a multitrillion-dollar gap between infrastructure spending and the revenues needed to finance it.

"Data centre bonds are having their Darwin moment, where the weakest credits struggle to survive," said Ludovic Subran, chief investment officer at Germany's Allianz. "The surge in credit spreads following power and construction delays show that data centre debt is priced too tight for execution risk."

The price of debt issued by Blue Owl and Meta-backed special purpose vehicle Beignet Investor to fund the Hyperion project has slipped from above par in early July to a little under 91 cents on the dollar.

Separately, bonds backing two Hut 8-developed projects — one in Louisiana and another in Texas leased by Nvidia — have fallen to around 93 and 91 cents on the dollar respectively. Bonds for the Blackstone-owned QTS data centre in Georgia dubbed "Project Excalibur" and leased to Microsoft have slipped below 87 cents on the dollar.

Neocloud providers have been hit even harder. Bonds issued by CoreWeave have sunk below 75 cents on the dollar — prices typically considered distressed — pushing yields to nearly 16 per cent on Wednesday. The company's shares are down nearly 25 per cent over the past week, while rival Nebius has lost more than 20 per cent.

AI chip giant Nvidia, which has invested tens of billions of dollars in numerous neoclouds and AI start-ups, has itself shed more than $300bn in market value over the past week.

The rout has come as a report this week by tech consultancy Gartner predicted that 80 per cent of neoclouds would "cease independent operations" by 2030, because of a multitrillion-dollar gulf between the pace of capital spending and expected returns from AI.
